title: Certificate of Analysis vs Certificate of Conformance
description: A certificate of analysis shows test results for one batch; a certificate of conformance only states that goods meet requirements. Here is when each one is enough.

Certificate of analysis or certificate of conformance: what each one proves

Both documents carry a batch number and a signature, and both say the goods are acceptable. Only one of them shows the results, and that difference decides when each is enough.

What is the difference between a certificate of analysis and a certificate of conformance?

A certificate of analysis reports the actual test results for one specific batch against its specification, signed by the quality unit that released it. A certificate of conformance states that a product or lot meets stated requirements without showing test results. The first gives evidence you can check; the second gives an assurance you must trust.

Two documents often arrive with a shipment and are easy to mistake for each other. One is a certificate of analysis. The other is a certificate of conformance, sometimes called a certificate of compliance or a declaration of conformity. Both carry a product name, a batch or lot number and a signature, and both say, in one way or another, that the goods are acceptable. They do not prove the same thing, and a buyer who accepts one when the other was needed can find out only when a receiving quality unit or an inspector asks the question.

This article explains what each document records, when each one is normally expected, and what a buyer should do when a supplier offers the weaker of the two. It describes general practice. Which document your own regulator and your own specification require is a question for your market and your product type.

Certificate of analysis vs certificate of conformance: what is the difference?

The difference is between evidence and assurance. A certificate of analysis reports what the tests on one batch actually found. Each row names a test, gives the acceptance criterion from the specification, and states the result. A reader can put that table beside their own specification and check every line.

A certificate of conformance makes a statement instead. It says that the product or lot meets stated requirements, such as a drawing, a specification, a standard or a purchase order. It usually shows no results at all. The reader learns that the issuer considers the goods compliant, but not what was measured, by whom, or how close the goods came to any limit.

What a certificate of analysis carries

A certificate of analysis identifies the material and its grade, the batch with its dates, the manufacturer and the site that made and tested it, every test in the agreed specification with its criterion and result, and a dated release by the quality unit. Because it is tied to one batch and shows numbers where the tests give numbers, it is the document a buyer uses to compare batches and to spot drift over time.

What a certificate of conformance carries

A certificate of conformance identifies the product, the lot or order it covers, the requirement it claims to meet, and the person or organisation making the claim. A good one names the exact specification or drawing and its revision. A weak one says only that the goods conform to requirements, without saying which requirements, which leaves the buyer with very little to hold.

When is a certificate of conformance enough?

A certificate of conformance is common, and often accepted, where the product is made to a fixed design and the important controls happen during manufacture rather than in a final test of each lot. Many medical consumables, packaging components and finished devices fall into this group. For a sterile single use item, for example, the assurance comes from a validated process, and the lot documentation may include process records alongside a conformance statement.

Even then, a certificate of conformance is only as useful as the system behind it. It carries weight when the issuer works under a quality management system that the buyer has assessed, and when the requirement it cites is precise. Without that, it is a signature on a sentence.

For a medical device, a declaration of conformity is a separate and formal document under the relevant regulation. It is a manufacturer's statement that the device meets the regulatory requirements of a given market, and it is not the same as a lot certificate. A buyer should keep the two apart and not treat either as a substitute for the other.

A certificate of analysis shows you the results; a certificate of conformance asks you to trust them. For an API or an excipient, where your own release depends on batch results, a certificate of conformance alone does not replace a certificate of analysis.

Why is a certificate of conformance not enough for an API or excipient?

For active pharmaceutical ingredients and excipients, the buyer's own quality unit normally has to decide whether to accept each batch. That decision rests on test results compared with a specification, and often on the buyer's own identity testing as well. A statement that the material conforms gives the quality unit nothing to compare. It cannot show where a batch sits against its assay range or its impurity criteria, and it cannot support a trend across batches.

So when a supplier of an API or excipient offers only a certificate of conformance, the right response is to ask for the manufacturer's certificate of analysis for that batch. If the supplier cannot provide one, that tells you something about the supplier's access to the manufacturer, which is worth knowing before the order rather than after it.

Can one document do both jobs?

Yes. Many certificates of analysis end with a statement that the batch meets the stated specification, which is a conformance statement supported by the results above it. That combination is the strongest form, because the claim and the evidence sit on the same page. The reverse does not hold: adding the word analysis to the title of a document that shows no results does not turn it into a certificate of analysis.

Some suppliers issue both, a certificate of analysis for the material and a certificate of conformance against the purchase order. That is fine, provided the batch numbers match and each document names the same manufacturer and site.

How should a buyer state the requirement?

The simplest protection is to write it down before ordering. The purchase order, the specification or the quality agreement should say which document must travel with each batch, who must issue it, and what it must contain. If a certificate of analysis from the original manufacturer is required, say so. If a certificate of conformance is acceptable for a particular item, say which requirement it must cite and which revision. A supplier who has agreed to that in writing has far less room to send the wrong paper.

When the goods arrive, the receiving check is short. Look at the title, then look for a results table. A document with a table of tests, criteria and results for the named batch is a certificate of analysis, whatever it is called. A document with a single statement of compliance is a certificate of conformance, whatever it is called.

Frequently asked questions

Is a certificate of compliance the same as a certificate of conformance?

In most commercial use, yes. Both names describe a statement that goods meet stated requirements, usually without test results. What matters is not the name but the content: which requirement is cited, which lot is covered, and who signs. For medical devices, a declaration of conformity is a separate formal document and should not be confused with either.

Can a certificate of conformance replace a certificate of analysis for an API?

Not on its own. A buyer's quality unit normally decides whether to accept each batch of an API or excipient by comparing test results with a specification. A conformance statement gives it nothing to compare. Ask for the manufacturer's certificate of analysis for that batch, and treat a supplier who cannot provide one with caution.

What makes a certificate of conformance worth relying on?

Three things: it cites an exact requirement with its revision, it identifies the lot or order it covers, and it is issued under a quality management system the buyer has assessed. A conformance statement that names no requirement, or comes from a party with no visible quality system, gives very little assurance.

Should both documents be requested for the same shipment?

Sometimes. A supplier may issue a certificate of analysis for the material and a certificate of conformance against the purchase order. That is acceptable when the batch numbers match and both name the same manufacturer and site. State in the purchase order or quality agreement which documents must travel with each batch.
